proof_skeleton_nl: Treat d=0 separately. For d>0, first translate polynomiality of Q_{A,B,d}(q) into cyclotomic divisibility-count inequalities, and then into a Hall-type semigroup condition on every coordinate subset. Invoke the weighted existence theorem to obtain homogeneous equations of degrees A+1,...,A+d whose only common zero is the origin. Nullstellensatz then gives a finite-dimensional quotient, and a general commutative-algebra lemma turns the resulting d homogeneous equations into a homogeneous regular sequence. The standard weighted complete-intersection Hilbert-series formula finally identifies the quotient with Q_{A,B,d}(q).

steps.derives: If d = 0, then the theorem holds: S=Q, Q_{A,B,0}(q)=1, and the empty sequence of homogeneous polynomials is a homogeneous regular sequence whose quotient has Hilbert series 1.
steps.trivial_justification: Lemma L7 is exactly the d=0 case.

steps.derives: Assume d > 0 and Q_{A,B,d}(q) belongs to Q[q]. Then for every positive integer n, the number of indices j in {1,...,d} for which n divides B+j is at most the number of integers e in {A+1,...,A+d} for which n divides e.
steps.trivial_justification: This is the forward implication of Lemma L1 applied to Q(q)=Q_{A,B,d}(q).

steps.derives: Assume d > 0. For every nonempty subset J of {1,...,d}, if Sigma(J) = { sum_{j in J} m_j (B+j) : each m_j is a nonnegative integer }, then at least |J| of the integers A+1,...,A+d lie in Sigma(J).
steps.trivial_justification: Instantiate Lemma L2 with w_j=B+j and E={A+1,...,A+d}. Step B2 provides exactly the divisibility inequalities required by the lemma.

steps.derives: Assume d > 0. There exist homogeneous polynomials g_1,...,g_d in S = Q[x_1,...,x_d] with deg(g_i)=A+i for each i such that, over an algebraic closure of Q, the common zero locus of g_1,...,g_d in affine d-space is exactly the origin.
steps.trivial_justification: Apply Lemma L3 with k=Q, weights w_j=B+j, target degrees e_i=A+i, and S=Q[x_1,...,x_d]. The field Q is infinite, each B+j is positive, and because the numbers A+1,...,A+d are distinct, Step B3 implies that for every nonempty J the set of indices i with e_i in Sigma(J) has cardinality at least |J|.

steps.derives: Assume d > 0. The quotient S/(g_1,...,g_d) is finite-dimensional over Q.
steps.trivial_justification: Let I=(g_1,...,g_d). Because the g_i are homogeneous, I is homogeneous, and Step B4 says that the common zero locus of I over an algebraic closure is exactly the origin. Lemma L4 then gives finite-dimensionality of S/I.

steps.derives: Assume d > 0. The sequence g_1,...,g_d is a homogeneous regular sequence in S; equivalently, for each i the image of g_i in S/(g_1,...,g_{i-1}) is not a zero-divisor.
steps.trivial_justification: Apply Lemma L5 with k=Q, weights w_i=B+i, and the homogeneous elements g_i from Step B4. Step B5 supplies the finite-dimensional quotient hypothesis.

steps.derives: Assume d > 0. Setting f_i := g_i for i=1,...,d gives homogeneous elements f_1,...,f_d in S with deg(f_i)=A+i, and for each i the image of f_i in S/(f_1,...,f_{i-1}) is not a zero-divisor.
steps.trivial_justification: This is a direct renaming of the polynomials from Steps B4 and B6.

steps.derives: Assume d > 0. The quotient by the constructed sequence satisfies Hilb_{S/(f_1,...,f_d)}(q) = prod_{i=1}^d (1 - q^(A+i)) / prod_{i=1}^d (1 - q^(B+i)) = Q_{A,B,d}(q).
steps.trivial_justification: Apply Lemma L6 with k=Q, weights w_i=B+i, degrees e_i=A+i, and g_i=f_i. Step B7 gives the regular-sequence and degree hypotheses, and the displayed quotient is exactly the definition of Q_{A,B,d}(q).

steps.derives: Assume d > 0. There exist homogeneous polynomials f_1, ..., f_d in S = Q[x_1, ..., x_d] graded by deg(x_i)=B+i such that deg(f_i)=A+i for every i, and for each i the image of f_i in S/(f_1, ..., f_{i-1}) is not a zero-divisor. Moreover Hilb_{S/(f_1,...,f_d)}(q)=Q_{A,B,d}(q), so Q_{A,B,d}(q) is realized by a homogeneous regular sequence in the weighted polynomial ring with variable weights B+1, ..., B+d and relation degrees A+1, ..., A+d.
steps.trivial_justification: Step B7 gives homogeneous elements with the required degrees and successive non-zero-divisor property; that property is exactly the definition of a homogeneous regular sequence in this setting. Step B8 identifies the Hilbert series of the quotient by this sequence with Q_{A,B,d}(q), which yields the advertised realization statement.

steps.derives: For integers A, B, d with A >= B >= 0 and d >= 0, define Q_{A,B,d}(q) := prod_{i=1}^d (1 - q^(A+i)) / (1 - q^(B+i)), with the empty product equal to 1 when d = 0. Assume Q_{A,B,d}(q) belongs to Q[q]. Let S be the weighted polynomial ring Q[x_1, ..., x_d] graded by deg(x_i) = B+i; when d = 0 interpret S as Q. Then there exist homogeneous polynomials f_1, ..., f_d in S such that deg(f_i) = A+i for every i, and for each i the image of f_i in S/(f_1, ..., f_{i-1}) is not a zero-divisor. Equivalently, Q_{A,B,d}(q) is realized by a homogeneous regular sequence in a weighted polynomial ring with variable weights B+1, ..., B+d and relation degrees A+1, ..., A+d.
steps.trivial_justification: Again split into the exhaustive cases d=0 and d>0. Step B1 proves the exact claim in the empty-variable case, and Step B9 proves the exact claim in the positive-dimensional case. Since d >= 0, these two cases cover all possibilities.
